questions.q: Why does Tableau default to a Line mark type when you drag a date dimension to Columns and a measure to Rows?
options: Because a date field signals a sequence, and a line's job is showing how a value changes across that sequence
Because dates can only ever be plotted as lines in Tableau
Because Tableau always defaults to Line regardless of field type
Because line charts require fewer computing resources than bar charts
questions.explain: Dates are the one field type that nudges Tableau's automatic mark-type guess toward Line, since lines are built to show a sequence of change.

questions.q: What is a dual-axis line chart, and when is it useful?
options: Two measures plotted on two independent scales sharing one horizontal axis — useful when the measures have very different magnitudes
Two entirely separate charts placed side by side with no shared axis
A chart type only available for geographic data
A line chart that can only display exactly two data points
questions.explain: A dual-axis view gives each measure its own independent scale while sharing the same horizontal timeline, which prevents a much larger measure from flattening a smaller one.

questions.q: How do you turn a dual-axis line view into a blended-axis view in Tableau?
options: Drag one measure from Rows directly onto the other measure's existing axis so both share a single scale
Right-click the view and select 'Blend Axes' from a context menu
Blended axes are the default and cannot be changed to dual-axis
Change the mark type from Line to Bar
questions.explain: Dragging one measure onto the other's axis blends them onto a single shared scale — useful when the two measures are close enough in magnitude to compare directly.

questions.q: What does the filled region in a stacked area chart actually change about how the chart reads, compared to a plain line chart?
options: It shifts the viewer's focus from the shape of change toward the cumulative volume and composition of the whole at each point in time
It has no effect — area and line charts are read identically
It makes individual series easier to compare precisely than a line chart would
It converts the measure from continuous to discrete
questions.explain: A stacked area chart's filled bands draw attention to total volume and composition over time, at the cost of making precise comparisons between individual bands harder than reading separate lines.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should you generally prefer multiple lines over a stacked area chart?
options: When precise comparison between individual series matters more than conveying a sense of total cumulative volume
Whenever the dataset has more than one dimension
Only when working with geographic data
Stacked area charts should always be preferred over lines when more than one measure is involved
questions.explain: Judging a band's thickness in the middle of a stack is harder than reading a line's height against a shared baseline, so multiple lines win when precision between series matters most.
